elements.name: Hydrogen
elements.uses: Fuel, water and ammonia production, rocket propellant, petroleum refining
elements.hazards: Extremely flammable; forms explosive mixtures with air; cryogenic liquid causes severe burns
elements.summary: The most abundant element in the universe, yet a gas at room temperature. A diatomic H2 molecule gives it an unusually low density for a gas.

elements.name: Helium
elements.uses: Coolant for superconducting magnets, lifting gas, protective inert atmosphere, leak detection
elements.summary: Discovered in the solar spectrum before it was found on Earth, helium is the second most abundant element in the universe and never freezes at ordinary pressure.

elements.name: Lithium
elements.uses: Rechargeable batteries, aluminium-lithium alloys, mood stabilising medication, heat-resistant glass
elements.hazards: Highly reactive with water and air; lithium metal fires cannot be extinguished with water
elements.summary: The lightest metal, soft enough to cut with a knife and low enough in density to float on water. Its name comes from the Greek word for stone.

elements.name: Beryllium
elements.uses: X-ray windows, lightweight alloys, copper-beryllium springs, spacecraft mirrors
elements.hazards: Inhaled dust causes chronic beryllium disease; it is a confirmed human carcinogen
elements.summary: A light, stiff, grey metal that is transparent to X-rays. It has the highest neutron yield of any light element, which is why it is used as a neutron source.

elements.name: Boron
elements.discoverer: Sir Humphry Davy, Joseph-Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis-Jacques Thenard
elements.uses: Heat-resistant borosilicate glass, detergents, fertilisers, control rods in nuclear reactors
elements.hazards: Toxic to plants at high concentration; borates harm the male reproductive system
elements.summary: Boron is a semiconductor metalloid whose electron-deficient bonding makes it a building block of sturdy borosilicate glass. It is essential to plant cell walls.

elements.name: Carbon
elements.uses: Steel making, fuels, diamond tools, activated carbon filters, carbon dioxide capture
elements.hazards: Fine carbon dust causes pneumoconiosis; graphite is a conductor and can overheat
elements.summary: The backbone of all organic chemistry: it bonds to itself in chains, rings and sheets. Diamond is its hardest allotrope and graphite the softest, both made of pure carbon.

elements.name: Nitrogen
elements.uses: Fertiliser, inert atmosphere, food packaging, liquid nitrogen coolant, explosives
elements.hazards: Asphyxiates by displacing oxygen; liquid nitrogen causes cold burns
elements.summary: Makes up 78 percent of air as a nearly inert diatomic gas. Fixing atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia feeds roughly half the world population.

elements.name: Oxygen
elements.discoverer: Joseph Priestley and Carl Wilhelm Scheele
elements.uses: Respiration, steel making, medical oxygen, water treatment, rocket oxidiser
elements.hazards: Supports combustion violently; enriched oxygen is a fire and explosion hazard
elements.summary: About 21 percent of air, needed by every living cell for aerobic respiration. In compounds such as water and carbon dioxide it is usually the most electronegative partner.

elements.name: Fluorine
elements.uses: Toothpaste, uranium enrichment, refrigerant chemicals, non-stick coatings
elements.hazards: The most reactive element; severe burns, toxic by every route, violently reacts with almost everything
elements.summary: The most electronegative and most oxidising element, a pale yellow gas that attacks glass. It is the element with the strongest pull on bonding electrons.

elements.name: Neon
elements.uses: Neon advertising signs, glow lamps, high-voltage indicators, cryogenic coolant
elements.summary: A glowing red-orange gas that glows when an electric discharge passes through it. It is completely inert because its filled outer shell gives it no reason to react.

elements.name: Sodium
elements.uses: Sodium-vapour lamps, table salt, sodium hydroxide soap, liquid-metal heat pipes
elements.hazards: Reacts violently with water and skin; sodium hydroxide is strongly corrosive
elements.summary: A soft silvery metal one third the density of water. Its brilliant yellow flame test is one of the most recognisable in chemistry.

elements.name: Magnesium
elements.uses: Lightweight alloys, fireworks, antacids, magnesium flares, desulphurisation of steel
elements.hazards: Magnesium ribbon and powder burn with an intense white flame
elements.summary: A light metal that burns with a brilliant white light. In seawater it is present as the Mg2+ ion, the second most abundant cation in the ocean.

elements.name: Aluminium
elements.uses: Aircraft and packaging foil, overhead power lines, cookware, catalysts, window frames
elements.hazards: Fine powder is a serious fire and explosion risk; the metal reacts with strong alkali
elements.summary: The most abundant metal in Earth crust. A thin, tough oxide film protects it so well that it is used for everything from cooking foil to spacecraft.

elements.name: Silicon
elements.uses: Semiconductors and microchips, silicones, glass, solar cells, computer chips
elements.hazards: Crystalline silica dust causes silicosis and lung cancer
elements.summary: The second most abundant element in Earth crust. Sand is mostly silicon dioxide, and ultrapure silicon is the base material of every computer chip.

elements.name: Phosphorus
elements.uses: Fertiliser, detergents, flame retardants, safety matches, nutritional supplements
elements.hazards: White phosphorus is acutely toxic, pyrophoric and a suspected carcinogen
elements.summary: The first element ever discovered that was unknown to the ancients. Its glowing white and red allotropes are highly reactive, while phosphate is central to DNA and energy transfer.

elements.name: Sulfur
elements.uses: Fertiliser and pesticides, sulphuric acid, gunpowder, rubber vulcanisation, matches
elements.hazards: Sulphur dust is an irritant; burning it produces toxic SO2
elements.summary: A bright yellow brittle solid known since prehistory and now the villain of acid rain. Its S8 ring can be opened and re-formed in almost any reaction.

elements.name: Chlorine
elements.uses: Water disinfection, PVC and solvents, bleach, hydrochloric acid, pharmaceuticals
elements.hazards: Toxic gas that destroys the lungs; reacts explosively with hydrogen, ammonia and water
elements.summary: A pungent green-yellow gas used to keep swimming pools safe. Chloride ions are essential for stomach acid and for fluid balance.

elements.name: Argon
elements.discoverer: Lord Rayleigh and Sir William Ramsay
elements.uses: Welding shielding gas, light bulbs, inert atmospheres, cryogenics, geochronology dating
elements.summary: The most abundant noble gas in air, discovered because its density did not fit nitrogen and oxygen. Argon is used whenever an atmosphere must stay completely unreactive.

elements.name: Potassium
elements.uses: Fertiliser, potassium hydroxide soap, table salt substitute, safe explosives
elements.hazards: Reacts violently with water and can ignite spontaneously when oxidised; severe skin and eye burns
elements.summary: A soft silvery alkali metal whose lilac flame is used to detect it in the presence of sodium. Potassium ions are essential for nerve function and fluid balance.

elements.name: Calcium
elements.uses: Quicklime and plaster, cement, dietary supplements, limestone scrubbing, bone and shell
elements.hazards: Reacts with water; quicklime causes severe chemical burns and calcium dust irritates the lungs
elements.summary: A soft silvery metal found as limestone, gypsum and shell. The orange-red flame test and the quicklime reaction are its signatures in the lab.

elements.name: Scandium
elements.uses: Aluminium-scandium alloys for aerospace, sports equipment and bicycle frames, metal halide lamps
elements.hazards: Scandium dust is flammable and mildly toxic; compounds should not be inhaled
elements.summary: A rare, light transition metal predicted by Mendeleev before it was found. Adding a little of it to aluminium makes a remarkably strong, light alloy.

elements.name: Titanium
elements.uses: Aircraft and jet engine parts, medical implants, white pigment, jewellery, armour plate
elements.hazards: Titanium powder and swarf are pyrophoric; the dioxide dust is a nuisance irritant
elements.summary: As strong as steel at half the weight, titanium is biocompatible enough for bone implants. Its white pigment paints everything from skyscrapers to toothpaste.

elements.name: Vanadium
elements.uses: Microalloyed steel, vanadium redox flow batteries, titanium alloys, catalysts
elements.hazards: Vanadium pentoxide dust is toxic and a suspected carcinogen; compounds are harmful to aquatic life
elements.summary: A tough metal whose multicoloured compounds made it a favourite of the nineteenth century. It hardens steel and holds the charge in large flow batteries.

elements.name: Chromium
elements.uses: Stainless steel, chrome plating, pigments, leather tanning, dichromate reagents
elements.hazards: Hexavalent chromium is a potent carcinogen and skin sensitiser; Cr(III) is far less harmful
elements.summary: Named for its colourful compounds, chromium gives stainless steel its corrosion resistance and rubies their red colour. It is also essential in small amounts to human health.

elements.name: Manganese
elements.uses: Steel alloy for rails and hardeners, dry cell batteries, manganese dioxide pigment, water treatment
elements.hazards: Chronic inhalation causes manganism, a Parkinson-like brain disease; the dust is a lung irritant
elements.summary: Essential for steelmaking and for removing oxygen and sulphur from molten iron. Too much manganese in the body produces the tremor disease manganism.

elements.name: Iron
elements.uses: Steel, construction, magnets, haemoglobin in blood, catalysts, rust pigments
elements.hazards: Rust weakens structures; iron dust is a respiratory hazard and iron overload causes haemochromatosis
elements.summary: The most abundant metal in Earth and the core of our planet. It carries oxygen in blood as haemoglobin, and its loss as rust costs billions every year.

elements.name: Cobalt
elements.uses: Rechargeable batteries, jet engine superalloys, hard metals, blue pigments, magnets
elements.hazards: Cobalt dust is a respiratory sensitiser and suspected carcinogen; some compounds cause skin allergy
elements.summary: The source of the deep blue in ancient glass and pottery. Cobalt superalloys hold turbine blades together and cobalt(II) ions make brilliant blue solutions.

elements.name: Nickel
elements.uses: Stainless steel, coinage, rechargeable batteries, catalysts, magnet alloys, plating
elements.hazards: A common contact allergen and carcinogen in nickel compounds; nickel carbonyl is extremely toxic
elements.summary: Found in meteorites as nickel-iron alloy, which is why it is a metal of the core. Its smoothness and corrosion resistance make it ideal for plating and coinage.

elements.name: Copper
elements.uses: Electrical wiring, plumbing, coins, bronze and brass alloys, heat exchangers, antifouling paint
elements.hazards: Copper sulphate harms aquatic life; copper fumes cause metal fume fever
elements.summary: The second best conductor of electricity after silver and one of the first metals humans used. It oxidises to a protective green patina that sheds rain and dust.

elements.name: Zinc
elements.uses: Galvanising steel, brass, zinc oxide paint and sunscreen, die casting, dietary supplements
elements.hazards: Zinc oxide fume causes metal fume fever; high doses of soluble zinc salts are toxic
elements.summary: A bluish-white metal used for centuries as a cosmetic and as brass. Modern galvanising protects steel with a sacrificial layer of zinc.

elements.name: Gallium
elements.uses: Semiconductors GaAs and GaN, gallium nitride LEDs, low-melting alloys, thermometers
elements.hazards: Liquid gallium stains and embrittles aluminium
elements.summary: Named after France, it melts just above room temperature in your hand. Gallium arsenide and gallium nitride power fast LEDs and high-frequency electronics.

elements.name: Germanium
elements.uses: Semiconductors and infrared optics, fibre optic glass, polymerisation catalysts, solar cells
elements.hazards: Germanium metal and dioxide are moderately toxic; industrial exposure affects the kidneys and blood
elements.summary: Predicted by Mendeleev as eka-silicon, then found in 1886. Its semiconductor behaviour and infrared transparency made it vital to the first fibre optic cables.

elements.name: Arsenic
elements.uses: Semiconductors, wood preservatives, insecticides, gallium arsenide, pigments
elements.hazards: A well known poison and Group 1 carcinogen that damages skin and nerves
elements.summary: A notorious poison, yet also the semiconductor of gallium arsenide infrared LEDs. It sublimes at 887 K and only melts under pressure at 1090 K.

elements.name: Selenium
elements.uses: Glass decolourising, selenium photocells and solar cells, glass manufacture, animal feed supplements
elements.hazards: Toxic in excess; causes garlic breath odour and selenosis in grazing livestock
elements.summary: Its conductivity changes with light, which made selenium the basis of early photocopiers. It is an essential trace element but toxic in larger doses.

elements.name: Bromine
elements.uses: Flame retardants, drilling fluids, water treatment, photographic chemicals, dyes
elements.hazards: A corrosive, toxic liquid that burns skin and eyes; vapour is a severe respiratory irritant
elements.summary: The only nonmetal that is liquid at room temperature, a red-brown volatile liquid with a choking red-brown vapour.

elements.name: Krypton
elements.uses: High-performance window glazing, lighting, laboratory lasers, leak detectors, photographic flash
elements.summary: A colourless noble gas named after the hidden or secret ray. Older buildings use krypton-filled double windows because it conducts heat poorly.

elements.name: Rubidium
elements.uses: Rubidium vapour lamps, photocells, rubidium clocks, specialty glass
elements.hazards: Ignites spontaneously in air and reacts explosively with water; severe chemical burns
elements.summary: The second softest metal, discovered with the spectroscope by its deep red lines. It is used in atomic clocks because its transition is extremely sharp.

elements.name: Strontium
elements.uses: Pyrotechnic red flares, fireworks, ferrite magnets, glass, red warning lights
elements.hazards: Reacts with water and burns with a red flame; soluble strontium salts are irritants
elements.summary: Burns with a brilliant crimson flame, which is why it colours fireworks red. The town Strontian in Scotland gave the element its name.

elements.name: Yttrium
elements.uses: Yttrium aluminium garnet laser crystals, phosphors, ceramics, superconductors, neutron windows
elements.hazards: Yttrium dust and compounds are irritants to skin and lungs; finely divided powder is flammable
elements.summary: A silvery metal named after the Swedish village Ytterby, source of so many rare elements. Its oxide hosts the neodymium laser used in barcode readers.

elements.name: Zirconium
elements.uses: Nuclear reactor cladding, ceramic tiles, zirconia dental crowns, hip replacements, sandpaper
elements.hazards: Zirconium powder is highly pyrophoric; the metal reacts with steam and acids at high temperature
elements.summary: Almost transparent to neutrons, so it clads nuclear fuel rods. Zirconia, the hardest white ceramic known, is used to imitate diamond.

elements.name: Niobium
elements.uses: Superalloys for jet turbines, superconducting wires, capacitors, spacecraft alloys
elements.hazards: Dust is a respiratory irritant; the metal ignites in air at about 250 degrees C
elements.summary: A soft grey metal whose only ore, columbite, looks like a tree branch and whose name means niobium, the daughter of Niobe. Adding a little niobium to steel triples its strength.

elements.name: Molybdenum
elements.uses: Steel and cast iron alloys, catalysts, lubricants, electrodes, nuclear fuel cladding
elements.hazards: Molybdenum trioxide dust irritates the eyes and lungs; soluble molybdates are mildly toxic
elements.summary: A silvery metal that raises steel strength and heat resistance at high temperature. Its name comes from the Greek for lead, because its ore resembled lead ore.

elements.name: Technetium
elements.uses: Medical imaging tracer, corrosion-resistant steel alloy, anti-corrosion plating, nuclear waste studies
elements.hazards: All technetium isotopes are radioactive; it is handled only in trace amounts in shielded facilities
elements.summary: The lightest element with no stable isotopes, and the first artificially produced. Technetium-99m is the workhorse medical tracer used in millions of scans.

elements.name: Ruthenium
elements.uses: Platinum-group catalysts, hard disk coatings, jewellery alloy, chemical synthesis catalysts
elements.hazards: Ruthenium tetroxide is highly toxic, volatile and stains skin; the metal itself is low toxicity
elements.summary: A hard, corrosion-resistant platinum-group metal found in ores with the other platinums. Its tetroxide vapour is a powerful oxidant used in very small amounts.

elements.name: Rhodium
elements.uses: Three-way catalytic converters, platinum jewellery, rhodium-plated spark plugs, glass
elements.hazards: Tetracarbonyl and soluble rhodium compounds are toxic and can cause sensitisation
elements.summary: The most reflective of metals, rhodium gives a mirror finish that never tarnishes. It is also the priciest catalyst metal, worth cleaning car exhausts.

elements.name: Palladium
elements.uses: Hydrogen purification, automotive catalysts, electronics plating, dental alloys, chemical coupling
elements.hazards: Palladium salts are irritants and can cause dermatitis; metal is not itself toxic
elements.summary: The metal with the lowest melting point of all the platinum group, and the only one with a partly filled d shell. It soaks up hydrogen like a sponge.

elements.name: Silver
elements.uses: Photographic film, jewellery, silverware, solar panels, antimicrobial coatings, electrical contacts
elements.hazards: Silver nitrate stains skin and is corrosive; dissolved silver salts are toxic to aquatic life
elements.summary: The best conductor of electricity of any element, and a soft metal that tarnishes black in air. Silver iodide seed clouds were used to seed rain before modern cloud seeding.

elements.name: Cadmium
elements.uses: Rechargeable batteries, yellow pigments, neutron absorbers in control rods, low-melting alloys
elements.hazards: Extremely toxic cumulative poison causing kidney and bone damage; a Group 1 carcinogen
elements.summary: A soft bluish metal named after the Latin cadmia, and long the pigment artists called cad yellow. It absorbs neutrons, which is why reactor control rods use it.

elements.name: Indium
elements.uses: Indium tin oxide touch screens, low-melting alloys, solder, infrared detectors, LED lenses
elements.hazards: Indium compounds damage the lungs and kidneys; dust exposure should be avoided
elements.summary: A soft, silvery metal that wets and clings to other metals like grease. Extremely thin films of indium tin oxide make the glass in a touchscreen conduct electricity.

elements.name: Tin
elements.uses: Solder, tin plating, bronze, tin cans, float glass, superconducting alloys
elements.hazards: Organic tin compounds disrupt the nervous system; inorganic tin is safer
elements.summary: One of the first metals humans used, known as a component of bronze. Its alloy with copper, pewter, and its low melting point still make it indispensable for soldering.

elements.name: Antimony
elements.uses: Flame retardants, lead-acid battery hardeners, bearings, semiconductor dopant, antimony iodide
elements.hazards: Antimony compounds are toxic like arsenic; stibine gas is highly poisonous and flammable
elements.summary: A brittle metalloid that hardens lead and stops it creeping, and whose compounds have coloured glass and pottery for millennia.

elements.name: Tellurium
elements.uses: Freeze-dry switches in cars, thermoelectric materials, solar film, rubber vulcanising, electronics
elements.hazards: Tellurium compounds cause a persistent garlic odour on the breath and are toxic in excess
elements.summary: A rare, brittle metalloid that changes conductivity with light, once used in the first self-referencing antifreeze device.

elements.name: Iodine
elements.uses: Iodised salt, disinfectants, X-ray contrast media, thyroid treatment, LCD polarising film
elements.hazards: Iodine vapour burns the eyes and airways; elemental iodine is toxic if swallowed
elements.summary: A blue-black solid that sublimes to a violet vapour. About a fifth of the average human body is the hormone thyroxine, which is made from dietary iodine.

elements.name: Xenon
elements.uses: Flash lamps for photography, ion propulsion, anaesthesia, plasma tubes, neutrino detectors
elements.summary: The heaviest of the noble gases that is still reasonably abundant, and the first to be made to react. It glows blue under electric discharge and fills modern flash bulbs.

elements.name: Caesium
elements.uses: Atomic clocks, caesium vapour photoelectric cells, rocket propellant, drilling fluid
elements.hazards: Reacts explosively with water and air; must be stored under oil
elements.summary: Named for the intense blue of its flame. Caesium-133 defines the second, because its hyperfine transition is so perfectly regular.

elements.name: Barium
elements.uses: Barium sulfate contrast medium for X-rays, drilling fluid, glass and ceramic frits, fireworks greens
elements.hazards: Soluble barium salts are acutely toxic; barium sulfate is harmless
elements.summary: A reactive silvery metal whose insoluble sulfate is famously harmless while the soluble carbonate is a poison. Barium ions glow apple green in a flame.

elements.name: Lanthanum
elements.uses: High-carbon-content steel, camera lens glass, fluid catalytic cracking catalysts, rechargeable batteries
elements.hazards: Dust is an irritant and may cause lung damage; lanthanum salts are low in toxicity
elements.summary: The element that gives the lanthanides their name, meaning stone-like. Its name in turn comes from the city of Ceres in Tuscany, where the mineral was found.

elements.name: Cerium
elements.discoverer: Jons Jacob Berzelius and Wilhelm Hisinger
elements.uses: Catalytic converters, glass polishing, camera exposure meters, lighter flints, gadolinium-free ceramics
elements.hazards: Dust is an irritant; the rare earth oxides are considered only mildly toxic
elements.summary: The most abundant of the rare earths, polishing glass and cleaning exhaust at the same time. Cerium readily flips between the +3 and +4 states, which is exactly what a catalyst needs.

elements.name: Praseodymium
elements.uses: Glass colouring, carbon arc electrodes, welding goggles, permanent magnets, catalytic converters
elements.hazards: Compounds are weakly toxic but dust should be handled with care
elements.summary: Named for its green spectral lines, the Greek leasios meaning green. A thin film of a praseodymium compound makes welding goggles that cut glare.

elements.name: Neodymium
elements.uses: Neodymium-iron-boron magnets, laser glass, headlamp glass, jewellery colouring
elements.hazards: Dust is a mild respiratory irritant; neodymium salts are of low toxicity
elements.summary: Its intense absorption bands give glass an eerie purple, and neodymium magnets are the strongest permanent magnets available, found in headphones and wind turbines.

elements.name: Promethium
elements.discoverer: J. A. Marinsky, L. E. Glendenin and C. D. Coryell
elements.uses: Nuclear batteries, luminous paint, thickness gauges, some lasers and X-ray sources
elements.hazards: All isotopes are radioactive; it must be handled in shielded and sealed containers
elements.summary: The only rare earth with no stable isotopes, so it is almost absent from nature. Its radioactive glow once made the numerals glow in watch dials.

elements.name: Samarium
elements.uses: Samarium-cobalt magnets, nuclear reactor control rods, cancer radiotherapy, infrared absorber in glass
elements.hazards: Compounds are of low toxicity, though soluble samarium salts irritate the skin and eyes
elements.summary: A rare earth with unusual magnetic properties, used in the strongest permanent magnets that work at high temperature. Sm-147 is naturally radioactive.

elements.name: Europium
elements.uses: Euro banknote anti-counterfeit ink, fluorescent lamp phosphors, LED phosphors, red and blue phosphors
elements.hazards: Low toxicity but should not be ingested; the dust is a mild irritant
elements.summary: A phosphor of the future: europium gives screens their reds and blues, and it was the first commercial fluorescent material to be exploited.

elements.name: Gadolinium
elements.uses: MRI contrast agents, neutron shielding, scintillator crystals, magnetic refrigeration
elements.hazards: Free gadolinium ions are toxic; chelates must be used for medical imaging
elements.summary: The only lanthanide and one of very few elements that are strongly paramagnetic, which is why it makes the gadolinium in MRI contrast agents.

elements.name: Terbium
elements.uses: Green phosphors in displays, magnetostrictive alloys, sonar, solid-state memory devices
elements.hazards: Low toxicity but dust exposure should be limited
elements.summary: Named after Ytterby, it was the element that showed magnetism could be traced to individual f electrons, an insight that won the twentieth-century quantum view of matter.

elements.name: Dysprosium
elements.uses: Neodymium magnet alloys, electric motor magnets, control rods in reactors, laser glass
elements.hazards: Low toxicity; the dust is a mild irritant; Lu-176 is very weakly radioactive
elements.summary: The hardest of the rare earth metals, added to neodymium magnets so they keep working in hot electric motors. The name means hard to get at.

elements.name: Holmium
elements.uses: Holmium laser for prostate surgery, colour filters for welding glass, magnetic flux concentrators
elements.hazards: Low toxicity; the dust is an irritant
elements.summary: Has the highest magnetic moment of any naturally occurring element, and it powers the green lasers surgeons use to break up kidney stones.

elements.name: Erbium
elements.uses: Erbium fibre optical amplifiers, glass colouring, nuclear reactor control rods, laser alloys
elements.hazards: Low toxicity; dust is a mild respiratory irritant
elements.summary: It gave the name to the erbium lasers that boost light in long-distance fibre optic cables, making internet traffic possible over thousands of kilometres.

elements.name: Thulium
elements.uses: Portable X-ray sources, surgical lasers, nuclear reactor control rods, red phosphor in glass
elements.hazards: Low toxicity but the dust is irritating
elements.summary: The rarest of the stable rare earths, named after Thule, an ancient name for the far north, because it came from a Greenland mineral.

elements.name: Ytterbium
elements.uses: Pressure transducers, fibre optic amplifiers, mechanical bearings, solar cell glass
elements.hazards: Low toxicity; the dust is a mild irritant; Lu-176 is very weakly radioactive
elements.summary: A soft metal whose simple electron configuration makes it a favourite in pressure sensors, and one of only two elements with three electronic configurations.

elements.name: Lutetium
elements.discoverer: Georges Urbain, Carl Auer von Welsbach and James Dewar
elements.uses: PET scanner detectors, catalysts for polymerisation, garnet laser crystals, oil refinery catalysts
elements.hazards: Low toxicity; finely divided powder may be flammable (weakly radioactive: 71-176, t½ 3.78 × 10¹⁰ y)
elements.summary: The last and hardest lanthanide, and the most stable of their isotopes. Lutetium oxyorthosilicate crystals detect gamma rays inside the body in PET scanners.

elements.name: Hafnium
elements.discoverer: Dirk Coster and George de Hevesy
elements.uses: Nuclear reactor control rods, superalloys, plasma cutting electrodes, high temperature alloys
elements.hazards: Hafnium dust is pyrophoric and the metal ignites in air; it is a suspected carcinogen
elements.summary: Zirconium and hafnium are so alike that Mendeleev called hafnium eka-zirconium. Because it soaks up neutrons, it makes perfect control rods.

elements.name: Tantalum
elements.uses: Capacitors for tiny electronics, surgical implants, chemical plant equipment, carbide cutting tools
elements.hazards: Tantalum dust is a respiratory irritant; the metal itself is biocompatible and nearly inert
elements.summary: Tantalum capacitors fit into watches and mobile phones because the oxide dielectric self-heals. The metal is so unreactive that it is used in surgical implants.

elements.name: Tungsten
elements.uses: Light bulb filaments, cutting tool tips, heavy alloys, radiation shielding, electrode contacts
elements.hazards: Tungsten carbide dust causes hard-metal lung disease; the metal itself is of low toxicity
elements.summary: The English name comes from Swedish tungsten heavy stone, while the symbol is from wolfram, the wolf that devoured tin during smelting. It melts higher than any metal.

elements.name: Rhenium
elements.discoverer: Walter Noddack, Ida Tacke and Otto Berg
elements.uses: Jet engine superalloys, platinum-rhenium catalysts, thermocouples, high-temperature coatings
elements.hazards: Rhenium compounds irritate the skin and lungs; Re-187 is very weakly radioactive (weakly radioactive: 75-187, t½ 4.12 × 10¹⁰ y)
elements.summary: The last stable element discovered in the 1920s, found in platinum ores as tiny amounts of the rarest isotope. It lets jet turbines run hotter and higher.

elements.name: Osmium
elements.uses: Fountain pen nibs, instrument pivots, electrical contacts, jewellery plating, catalysts
elements.hazards: Osmium tetroxide vapour is extremely toxic and damages the eyes, skin and lungs
elements.summary: The densest of all naturally occurring elements, and the metal whose powder smells sharp and sweet. Its tetroxide is used in microscopic amounts for staining fat.

elements.name: Iridium
elements.uses: Catalysts for ammonia synthesis, crucibles for melting very high melting point metals, spark plugs, implants
elements.hazards: Some iridium salts irritate the skin; the metal and its bio-inert oxide are safe
elements.summary: The most corrosion-resistant metal known, and the one whose worldwide iridium layer marks the end of the dinosaurs. It melts above 2400 degrees C.

elements.name: Platinum
elements.uses: Catalytic converters, laboratory crucibles and electrodes, chemotherapy drug cisplatin, jewellery
elements.hazards: Cisplatin and platinum salts are highly toxic and are handled as cytotoxic drugs
elements.summary: Precious, unreactive and soft enough to work by hand, platinum is the classic laboratory metal. Its surface catalysis in converters cuts carbon monoxide emissions dramatically.

elements.name: Gold
elements.uses: Electronics contacts, bullion and coins, jewellery, dentistry, gold nanoparticles in diagnostics
elements.hazards: Barely toxic, but gold salts can cause dermatitis
elements.summary: The classic noble metal: unreactive, malleable and the only yellow element of the metals. One tonne of seawater holds about 4 grams, which is why gold is also a measure of abundance.

elements.name: Mercury
elements.uses: Thermometers, barometers, fluorescent lamps, electrical switches, dental amalgam
elements.hazards: A potent neurotoxin that damages the brain and kidneys
elements.summary: The only metal that is liquid at room temperature, used for thousands of years in thermometers. A single spilled drop of mercury begins a long-lived contamination of the environment.

elements.name: Thallium
elements.uses: Infrared optics, semiconductor detectors, high temperature alloys, rat poison, low melting glass
elements.hazards: Extremely toxic in small doses; damages nerves and causes hair loss
elements.summary: A soft, blue-grey metal once sold as rat poison and now used where nothing else survives the heat. Its name comes from the bright green line in its spectrum.

elements.name: Lead
elements.uses: Radiation shielding, car batteries, solder, plumbing, paint and pigments, shot and diving weights
elements.hazards: A powerful neurotoxin that damages the brain and kidneys, especially dangerous to children and fetuses
elements.summary: One of the four elements known since prehistory, and the heaviest of them. Its density, softness and shielding make it perfect for pipes and radiation aprons, but it poisons children readily.

elements.name: Bismuth
elements.uses: Pepto-Bismol stomach remedy, low melting alloys and fuses, lead-free shot, semiconductor compounds
elements.hazards: Soluble bismuth salts are toxic to the kidneys; the metal itself is of low toxicity
elements.summary: One of the few elements that is slightly less dense than water, and the heaviest of all elements that are essentially stable. Its iridescent stair-stepped crystals are easy to grow.

elements.name: Polonium
elements.discoverer: Marie Sklodowska Curie and Pierre Curie
elements.uses: Neutron source in early nuclear reactors, anti-static polonium-210 sources in industrial detectors
elements.hazards: Intensely radioactive, self-heating and toxic if inhaled or swallowed; it contaminates surfaces it touches
elements.summary: Discovered by Marie Curie, who named it for her homeland Poland. It gives off a blue glow of its own radiation and is lethal in microgram amounts.

elements.name: Astatine
elements.discoverer: Dale R. Corson, Kenneth R. MacKenzie and Emilio Segre
elements.uses: Experimental thyroid cancer treatment and radiopharmaceutical research only
elements.hazards: Intensely radioactive and the rarest natural element; always sealed
elements.summary: So rare that only a few atoms exist in the crust at any time. It is the heaviest halogen and would be a solid, black metal rather than a gas.

elements.name: Radon
elements.uses: Seismology tracer, neutron source, radiotherapy of some tumours
elements.hazards: Radioactive; seeps from rock into basements and causes lung cancer
elements.summary: A heavy, colourless noble gas produced by the decay of radium in rocks. Because it is radioactive and heavier than air it collects in the lowest rooms of a house.

elements.name: Francium
elements.uses: No commercial uses; studied only as a research curiosity and in medical isotope experiments
elements.hazards: So radioactive that a visible sample would destroy itself by its own decay heat
elements.summary: The least stable of the first 101 elements, with a half-life of only 22 minutes. Never more than about 30 grams of it exist in the whole crust at any moment.

elements.name: Radium
elements.discoverer: Marie Sklodowska Curie and Pierre Curie
elements.uses: Historic luminous paints, radiotherapy for cancer in the early twentieth century, some industrial radiography
elements.hazards: Highly radioactive bone seeker; contaminates soil and water
elements.summary: Marie Curie isolated radium from pitchblende and glowed in the dark from it. It is chemically a simple alkaline earth metal, far more reactive than barium.

elements.name: Actinium
elements.uses: Radioactive tracer, detector for neutron flux, research on the early actinides
elements.hazards: Radioactive; Ac-227 glows pale blue and is a strong gamma emitter
elements.summary: Named after the actinium series it begins, and about 150 times more radioactive than radium. Only tiny amounts have ever been isolated.

elements.name: Thorium
elements.uses: Nuclear fuel for molten salt and high temperature reactors, thoriated tungsten welding electrodes, mantle lamps
elements.hazards: Radioactive and chemically irritating; must be handled under licence
elements.summary: Three or four times as abundant as uranium in the crust, and the only naturally occurring isotope lasts longer than the universe. It is a candidate fuel for molten salt reactors.

elements.name: Protactinium
elements.discoverer: Kasimir Fajans and Oswald Helmuth Gohring
elements.uses: Research on actinide chemistry, nuclear fuel studies
elements.hazards: Highly radioactive and very toxic if inhaled; it decays to actinium-227 within weeks
elements.summary: A rare, expensive metal sitting between thorium and uranium in the decay chain. Its name means before actinium, because it decays into it.

elements.name: Uranium
elements.uses: Nuclear fuel, depleted uranium counterweights and radiation shielding, dating rocks by uranium decay
elements.hazards: Radioactive, chemically a kidney toxin, and it can be enriched into weapons material
elements.summary: The heaviest naturally occurring element, a dense silvery metal whose U-235 fission releases the energy of a star. Klaproth first found it in the mineral pitchblende in 1789.

elements.name: Neptunium
elements.uses: Nuclear reactor fuel and plutonium production, neutron detectors, tracer studies
elements.hazards: Radioactive and a recognised carcinogen; it is fissile with U-238 and must be strictly controlled
elements.summary: The first transuranium element made, named after the planet beyond Uranus because of where uranium ended and neptunium began.

elements.name: Plutonium
elements.discoverer: Glenn T. Seaborg, Edwin McMillan, Joseph W. Kennedy and Arthur C. Wahl
elements.uses: Nuclear weapons and reactor fuel, radioisotope thermoelectric generators in space probes
elements.hazards: Highly radioactive, a potent bone marrow toxin, and pyrophoric in finely divided form
elements.summary: A silvery metal named for Pluto and first made in a cyclotron. Different isotopes span from thousands of years to tens of thousands of years of half life.

elements.name: Americium
elements.discoverer: Glenn T. Seaborg, Ralph A. James, Leon O. Morgan and Albert Ghiorso
elements.uses: Smoke detectors, alpha particle sources in instruments, X-ray fluorescence spectrometers
elements.hazards: Radioactive bone seeker; handling requires shielding and strict contamination control
elements.summary: A metal discovered during the Manhattan Project and named for the Americas. A gram of Am-241 powers every household smoke detector, emitting a harmless alpha particle that sets off an alarm.

elements.name: Curium
elements.discoverer: Glenn T. Seaborg, Ralph A. James and Albert Ghiorso
elements.uses: Alpha particle sources in space probes, calibration standards, cancer radiotherapy research
elements.hazards: Radioactive and highly toxic; handling requires remote and shielded equipment
elements.summary: Named after Marie and Pierre Curie, and the element that powered the alpha particle instruments on the Viking and Mars rover landers.

elements.name: Berkelium
elements.discoverer: Glenn T. Seaborg, Stanley G. Thompson and Albert Ghiorso
elements.uses: Production of the heavier elements such as tennessine, research in high energy physics
elements.hazards: Radioactive, and so scarce that only microgram quantities have ever been produced
elements.summary: The last element to be made by the milligram amounts of the original laboratory team, and named after the town of Berkeley, California.

elements.name: Californium
elements.discoverer: Stanley G. Thompson, Kenneth Street Jr., Albert Ghiorso and Glenn T. Seaborg
elements.uses: Neutron source for starting up nuclear reactors, neutron activation analysis, cancer radiotherapy
elements.hazards: Extremely radioactive and dangerous if inhaled; it is a serious bone seeker
elements.summary: The most useful synthetic element on Earth: a fragment the size of a grain emits millions of neutrons every second, used to find gold and silver in ore and to start reactors.

elements.name: Einsteinium
elements.discoverer: Albert Ghiorso and colleagues at Berkeley
elements.uses: Studies of the heaviest elements, target material in nuclear physics research
elements.hazards: Highly radioactive; produced in microgram quantities that decay to einsteinium-253 in months
elements.summary: Found in the fallout of the first hydrogen bomb test, and named for Albert Einstein. Its metal was produced in tiny amounts in 1961 and weighed with extraordinary care.

elements.name: Fermium
elements.discoverer: Albert Ghiorso and colleagues at Berkeley
elements.uses: Basic research on heavy nuclei and superheavy element chemistry
elements.hazards: Radioactive with a half life of about 100 days; never made in weighable amounts
elements.summary: The heaviest element that can be made by neutron bombardment, and the heaviest element that can be formed in supernovae. Named for Enrico Fermi.

elements.name: Mendelevium
elements.discoverer: Albert Ghiorso, Stanley G. Harvey, Glenn T. Seaborg, Kenneth Choppin and Stanley G. Thompson
elements.uses: Research into superheavy element chemistry and ion exchange separation
elements.hazards: Radioactive with a half life of 51 days; studied as individual atoms only
elements.summary: The first element to be studied one atom at a time, using methods that revealed it behaves chemically like the lighter rare earths.

elements.name: Nobelium
elements.discoverer: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research, Dubna, and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory
elements.uses: Research into superheavy element properties, chemical comparison with lanthanides
elements.hazards: Radioactive with a 58 minute half life; only detectable a few atoms at a time
elements.summary: The first element produced in a laboratory by collecting atoms, rather than weighing them. Its name honours Alfred Nobel.

elements.name: Lawrencium
elements.discoverer: Albert Ghiorso, Torbjorn Sikkeland, Atte Mohring and Isadore Perlman
elements.uses: Research into superheavy element structure, the heaviest actinide
elements.hazards: Radioactive; only a few atoms can be produced at a time in accelerator experiments
elements.summary: The last actinide and the eleventh transuranium element, discovered in debris from a hydrogen bomb test and named for Ernest Lawrence.

elements.name: Rutherfordium
elements.discoverer: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research, Dubna, and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory
elements.uses: Chemical studies of the heaviest elements, no practical applications yet
elements.hazards: Radioactive, produced atom by atom, and handled only in accelerator laboratories
elements.summary: The heaviest element with known chemical behaviour that resembles a group 4 metal, named for Ernest Rutherford, who discovered the nucleus.

elements.name: Dubnium
elements.uses: Theoretical chemistry of superheavy elements, accelerator research only
elements.hazards: Radioactive, short lived, and made only a few atoms at a time
elements.summary: Named after Dubna, the Russian research town where much of the heaviest element work was done. Its chemistry finally proved group 5 still behaves like niobium.

elements.name: Seaborgium
elements.uses: Theoretical and experimental superheavy element chemistry research
elements.hazards: Radioactive; only a handful of atoms have ever existed
elements.summary: The first element named after a living person, Glenn Seaborg, and evidence suggests it may not behave exactly like a straightforward group 6 metal.

elements.name: Bohrium
elements.uses: Experimental superheavy element chemistry research
elements.hazards: Radioactive, with a half life of only about a minute
elements.summary: Named for Niels Bohr, whose shell model explains the whole architecture of this periodic table. It was found at the heavy ion research centre in Darmstadt.

elements.name: Hassium
elements.uses: Theoretical and experimental superheavy element chemistry
elements.hazards: Radioactive, with half lives measured in seconds
elements.summary: Named for the German state of Hesse, home of the GSI laboratory. Its tetroxide, a whole group 8 chemistry fingerprint, was actually synthesised a few atoms at a time.

elements.name: Meitnerium
elements.uses: Experiments to see if it is a group 9 metal or a heavier platinum
elements.hazards: Radioactive, made only a few atoms at a time in accelerators
elements.summary: Named after Lise Meitner, who explained nuclear fission. The experiments show the heaviest platinum-like elements behave unlike their lighter homologues.

elements.name: Darmstadtium
elements.uses: Superheavy element structure and chemistry research
elements.hazards: Radioactive, with a half life measured in seconds
elements.summary: Named after Darmstadt, the German city of its discovery, and a member of the platinum group by position.

elements.name: Roentgenium
elements.uses: Superheavy element chemistry, discovered in a cyclotron
elements.hazards: Radioactive, made a few atoms at a time in a cyclotron
elements.summary: Named after Wilhelm Conrad Rontgen, who discovered X-rays. It sits in group 11 with copper, silver and gold, but its chemistry is still unknown.

elements.name: Copernicium
elements.uses: Theoretical study of relativistic effects on the heaviest atoms
elements.hazards: Radioactive, with a half life measured in seconds
elements.summary: Named after the astronomer Copernicus. Its very high ionisation energy suggests it may behave more like a noble gas or halogen than a mercury-like metal.

elements.name: Nihonium
elements.uses: Research into the properties of superheavy nuclei
elements.hazards: Radioactive, with a half life of a few seconds
elements.summary: The first element discovered in Asia, made in a cyclotron at RIKEN in Japan. Its name is Nihon, the Japanese name for Japan.

elements.name: Flerovium
elements.discoverer: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research, Dubna, and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
elements.uses: Experimental study of its unusually volatile atoms
elements.hazards: Radioactive, with a half life of only a couple of seconds
elements.summary: Named after the Flerov Laboratory, and set to join group 14. Its gold-coloured atoms behave more like a metal than a metal-like element should.

elements.name: Moscovium
elements.discoverer: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research, Dubna, and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
elements.uses: Research into the superactinide region of the periodic table
elements.hazards: Radioactive, with a half life of fractions of a second
elements.summary: Named for the Moscow region, where Dubna sits. It belongs to a predicted superactinide series whose chemistry is barely described by any table.

elements.name: Livermorium
elements.discoverer: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research, Dubna, and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
elements.uses: Experimental study of its chemistry and position in group 16
elements.hazards: Radioactive, with a half life of milliseconds
elements.summary: Named for the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California, which co-discovered it with Dubna.

elements.name: Tennessine
elements.discoverer: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research, Dubna, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
elements.uses: Research on whether it behaves as a metalloid like its lighter homologues
elements.hazards: Radioactive, decaying in tens of milliseconds
elements.summary: Named after Tennessee, home of the Oak Ridge laboratory. Calculations suggest it is a solid metalloid, not a gas like the other halogens.

elements.name: Oganesson
elements.discoverer: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research, Dubna, and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
elements.uses: Theoretical study of the heaviest atom known; no applications are possible
elements.hazards: Radioactive, with a half life of well under a millisecond
elements.summary: The heaviest element known and the last of the periodic table, named for Yuri Oganessian. Its nucleus is so large and loosely bound that it may not behave as a gas at all.
